full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff respondents filed a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land by evicting the defendants. The plaintiffs' case, in short is that the suit land was recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 160 of mouza Borai and the plaintiffs, by an amicable partition amongst themselves and pro-defendants, were possessing the same; that during the last c.s. operation Jasmat Sardar  was possessing the suit land as a barga darunder Girish Chandra and others, the plaintiffs predecessors, on delivering half of the produce of the land from year to year; and that during Jasmat Sardar's life time the land was taken and given borga bandabosta to others. As Jasmat was possessing the land as borgadar his name was wrongly recorded in the C.S. record as tenant paying borga rent though he was never recognized as a tenant by the plaintiffs' predecessors. Acting on rumors, that lands recorded in the names of bargadars paying half the produce as rent, had vested in the bargadar's ; defendants, 1, 2, and 3, got fraudulent kabala from Jasmat's daughters, defendants 4 and 5 and forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff's from the suit land in Baishak, 1364 B.S. and hence the suit. 

 6. Mr. A.T.M. Kamrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misinterpreted the decision in the case of Kumir Mondal Vs. Pramatha Nath Chowdhury (1962) in 14 DL:R 801 in as much as the principle laid down in the said case is that a borgadar recorded in the C.S. Khatian as tenant before the introduction of the proviso to clause (17) of section 3 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 by the amending Act of 1928 can plead tenancy right even after the introduction of the proviso. He has further submitted that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the C.S. Khatian cannot be held to have been rebutted merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entry. Mr. Islam, in support of his contention, has relied on Alimuddin Munshi Vs. Mainuddin Talukdar (1962) 14 DLR 725. 

 9. The C.S. Khatian recorded Jasmat Sardar  as a borgadar as well as a rayotisthitiban under Girish Chandra Majumdar and others at a rental of half of the produces inclusive of cess. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that Jasmat took borga settlement by a kabuliyat (Ext. 1) for a term of 7 years from 1321 B.S. and the preparatory works of C.S. operation started in the locality after 1327 B.S. and the record of rights was finally published in 1925 corresponding to 1332 B.S. He has observed that "it is quite likely that the settlement operation actually began at a stage when the term of the barga lease did not expire. It is, therefore, clear borga has been mentioned in the khatian. In the absence of any other stipulation between the parties Jasmat would be deemed to have continued in possession as a borgadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in section 116 of the T.P. Act and as enunciated in principle in section 51 B.T. Act". 

 11. A finding as to a rebuttal of a statutory presumption is no doubt a finding of fact and it should not ordinarily be disturbed in second appeal. In the present case, however, the finding as to the rebuttal of the presumption of the C,S. record is based on a material mistaken assumption that Jasrnat Sardar would be deemed to have continued in possession as a bargadar on the principle of holding over as enunciated in Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and as enunciated in principle under section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has conceded that neither section 166 of the Transfer of Property Act nor section 51 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to a bargadar. He has, however, contended that the principle of holding over has been applied by way of analogy. The right of holding over, unless conferred by a statute, cannot be implied or inferred by analogy. Long five years after the terms of the borga kabuliyat expired, the C.S. Khatian was published on 6-9-25. The assumption of the Court of appeal below that the settlement operation actually began at the stage when the terms of the borga lease did not expire is based on no evidence. 

 The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this case, though relied on by the learned Munsif. For want of proper approach to the material question in the matter and non-appreciation of the evidence on the records particularly the evidence of the D.Ws. he has arrived at an erroneous decision. In the present case, apart from merely asserting that the C.S. Khatian was 'Wrongly recorded, the plaintiff did not adduce any other evidence in support of his contention. There was no averment that Jasmat continued to possess the land on the expiry of the terms of the kabuliyat on the same terms and conditions. In fact there is no mention of a borga kabuliyat in the plaint. On the other hand, defendant No.1, apart from relying on the C.S. record, produced Defendant 2, the Tahsildar of the landlords, who stated that at the time of C.S. operation he himself and another amin looked after the preparation of the C.S. record and the suit land belonged to Jasmat on payment of paddy lent to the landlords. This witness admitted the kabuliyat to be written in his hand. He further stated in cross-examination that he held some lands of the landlords as bargadar but his name was recorded as mere borgadar possessor with an entry in the rent column. 

 19. From the evidence on record it is clear that the predecessors of Defendant 1 never possessed the land as a bargadar of the plaintiffs and the defendant’s assertion that Jasmat and his heirs possessed the land in their own rights has been amply substantiated by the evidence on record. From Ext. 1it cannot be said, though contended by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, that the subsequent possession of Jasmat was one of a bargadar . I do not find any mention of the kabuliyat in the C.S. Khatian. The learned Subordinate Judge has assumed, on a total misrepresentation of evidence on the record, that since Jasmat died 6/7 years back the sui t is within twelve years of possession through a recorded bargadar. From the evidence on record it is clear that the plaintiffs had no possession within 12 years before the institution of suit. The learned Munsif rightly dismissed the suit.
